Dregs
DREGZ
noun (plural)
From the Norse dregg, sediment. The dregs are what lies at the bottom of a cup — the thick, bitter residue drunk last by the one who empties it, and therefore Scripture’s figure for the uttermost of wrath.

Biblical Definition

The dregs are the bottom of the cup, and Scripture builds one of its most terrible images upon them. “For in the hand of the LORD there is a cup, and the wine is red; it is full of mixture; and he poureth out of the same: but the dregs thereof, all the wicked of the earth shall wring them out, and drink them” (Psa 75:8). Two things are asserted: the cup is in God’s hand, and the wicked will drink it to the very bottom, wringing out the last of it. Isaiah turns the same figure upon Jerusalem — “thou hast drunken the dregs of the cup of trembling” (Isa 51:17), a city staggering like a drunkard under judgment. And then comes one of the great gospel reversals of the Old Testament. God says to that same city: “Behold, I have taken out of thine hand the cup of trembling, even the dregs of the cup of my fury; thou shalt no more drink it again” (Isa 51:22). The cup is not diluted, nor waived, nor set aside — it is taken out of her hand, which means someone else must hold it. The New Testament shows who. In Gethsemane the Son prays, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me, and then drinks it; and on the cross He does not stop partway. The dregs are the point. A Saviour who drank most of the cup would leave His people the bitterest part; He wrung it out.

Webster 1828 Definition

The sediment at the bottom of a cup; the last and bitterest portion, and hence in Scripture the uttermost measure of divine wrath.

DREGS, n. plural. The sediment of liquors; lees; grounds; feculence.

From the Norse dregg, sediment.

Waste or worthless matter; the most despicable part of anything.

In Scripture, the last and bitterest portion of the cup of wrath (Psa 75:8).

To wring out the dregs is to drain the vessel utterly.

Key Scripture

Psa 75:8 — "For in the hand of the LORD there is a cup, and the wine is red; it is full of mixture; and he poureth out of the same: but the dregs thereof, all the wicked of the earth shall wring them out, and drink them."

Isa 51:17 — "Awake, awake, stand up, O Jerusalem, which hast drunk at the hand of the LORD the cup of his fury; thou hast drunken the dregs of the cup of trembling, and wrung them out."

Isa 51:22 — "Thus saith thy Lord the LORD, and thy God that pleadeth the cause of his people, Behold, I have taken out of thine hand the cup of trembling, even the dregs of the cup of my fury; thou shalt no more drink it again:"

Mat 26:39 — "And he went a little further, and fell on his face, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt."

Modern Corruption

Penal substitution is widely dismissed as unworthy of God, but the cup imagery is Scripture’s own, and it is the same cup — taken from His people’s hand and drunk by the Son.

expand to see more

The corruption is the rejection of substitutionary wrath. It is now common to hear that a Father punishing a Son is unjust, even monstrous, and that the cross must instead be read as solidarity, example, or the exposure of violence. The dictionary rejects this and holds with the confession that Christ bore the wrath of God in the room and stead of His people. Note that the cup image is not a later theological construction imposed on the text; it is the Bible’s own vocabulary, running from Psa 75:8 through Isa 51 to Gethsemane, where our Lord Himself names what He is about to drink. Strip the wrath out and Isa 51:22 becomes unintelligible — God takes the cup out of thine hand, and it must then be in someone’s.

Recover the plain sense: the objection misconceives the parties. This is not an angry deity venting upon an unwilling third party, but the Son of God who volunteered before the world was, one in essence with the Father, laying down His life of Himself — no man taketh it from me. The Trinity is not divided at Calvary; it is unanimous. And take the comfort the dregs are there to give. Because He wrung the cup out, there is nothing left in it for those who are His. Rom 8:1 follows necessarily: there is therefore now no condemnation, not because condemnation was waived, but because it was drunk.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Norse dregg, sediment — the bitter bottom of the cup; wrath drunk to the last, and taken out of His people’s hand.

Dregs — Norse dregg, sediment; the thick residue of a cup.

Psa 75:8: the cup is in the hand of the LORD, and the wicked wring out the dregs.

Isa 51:17: Jerusalem staggering, having drunk the dregs of the cup of trembling.

Isa 51:22: God takes the cup out of thine hand — so another must hold it.

Mat 26:39: the Son prays over the cup and then drinks it.

Usage

"The cup imagery is Scripture’s own vocabulary, not a later theological import."

"Isa 51:22 requires a substitute: the cup is taken from one hand into another."

"Because the dregs were wrung out, there is nothing left in the cup for His people."
